content: The SI unit for luminous intensity is the candela (cd), which is one of the seven base units in the International System of Units (SI). The human eye is sensitive only to light within the visible spectrum, and its sensitivity varies depending on the wavelength of the light. Under bright lighting conditions, known as photopic vision, the human eye is most sensitive to light with a wavelength of approximately 555 nm, which appears greenish-yellow. Light of the same radiant intensity at other wavelengths will have a lower luminous intensity because the eye is less sensitive to those wavelengths. The sensitivity of the human eye to light across different wavelengths is represented by a standardized curve called the luminosity function, denoted as V(λ) or (overline{y}(lambda)). It is important to distinguish luminous intensity from other photometric quantities. Luminous intensity refers to the perceived power emitted per unit solid angle in a specific direction, whereas luminous flux represents the total perceived power emitted in all directions. The candela, as the SI unit of luminous intensity, has an operational definition based on a specific physical process. By definition, a light source that emits monochromatic light at a frequency of 540 THz (corresponding to a wavelength of approximately 555 nm) with a radiant intensity of 1/683 watts per steradian in a given direction will have a luminous intensity of one candela in that direction. The frequency of 540 THz is chosen because it corresponds to the peak sensitivity of the human eye under photopic conditions. If such a light source were to emit uniformly in all directions, the total radiant flux would be approximately 18.40 milliwatts, given that a sphere encompasses about 12.6 steradians. For reference, a typical candle emits roughly one candela of luminous intensity. Historically, the concept of luminous intensity has evolved. In 1881, Jules Violle proposed the Violle as a unit of luminous intensity. This was significant because it was the first unit of light intensity that did not rely on the properties of a specific lamp. However, the Violle was eventually replaced by the candela in 1946, which became the standardized unit. For monochromatic light of a specific wavelength (λ), the luminous intensity can be calculated using the formula: [ I_v = K_m cdot V(λ) cdot I_e ] where ( I_v ) is the luminous intensity, ( K_m ) is a constant representing the maximum luminous efficacy of radiation, ( V(λ) ) is the value of the luminosity function at the given wavelength, and ( I_e ) is the radiant intensity. When dealing with light that contains multiple wavelengths (as is typically the case), the luminous intensity is determined by summing or integrating over the spectrum of wavelengths present.
